# Sodium-Ion Batteries: The Hype vs. Reality

Learn what sodium-ion batteries can and can’t do yet, plus how they compare to lithium for real-world RV, solar, and off-grid power systems.

January 13, 2026

If you pay attention to energy-storage trends, it’s hard to miss the buzz around sodium-ion batteries. Between new product announcements and global supply-chain shifts, many are asking: *Is sodium-ion going to replace lithium-based batteries?*

At Battle Born Batteries, we take innovation seriously. Our in-house R&D department continuously evaluates emerging technologies and explores ways to improve both existing lithium iron phosphate systems and next-generation chemistries. We are genuinely excited about the potential of sodium-ion for certain applications. However, our testing and real-world analysis show that the technology is still far from ready to replace LiFePO₄ in RVs, off-grid homes, boats, vans, or any mobile deep-cycle system.

The characteristics of sodium-ion chemistry simply do not align with the performance demands of these environments, at least not yet.



---

## Key Takeaways (If You’re in a Hurry)

* **Sodium-ion batteries are interesting, but early.** The tech is real, but products are immature, especially in 12V/24V/48V formats used for RV and off-grid systems.
* **Voltage behavior is the biggest practical problem.** Sodium-ion’s wide voltage window and sloped discharge curve mean inverters often cut out early, so you can’t access the full rated capacity without custom hardware.
* **LiFePO₄ still wins on performance and life.** Sodium-ion batteries have lower efficiency and shorter practical cycle life than quality LiFePO₄ packs, which routinely deliver 3,000–5,000+ deep cycles.
* **Safety is comparable, not better.** Sodium-ion uses similar organic electrolytes and does not offer a clear safety advantage over LiFePO₄, which is already one of the most thermally stable and proven chemistries in low-voltage systems.
* **“Abundant sodium” doesn’t equal abundant, cheap battery packs—yet.** Battery-grade sodium-ion cells still depend on processing and manufacturing infrastructure that’s heavily concentrated in China and still scaling.
* **For RVs, marine applications, and off-grid cabins, LiFePO4 is still the clear winner.** Better energy density, better usable capacity, higher efficiency, and a mature ecosystem of chargers, inverters, and BMS technology exist today.

---



---

## What Exactly Are Sodium-Ion Batteries?

A sodium-ion battery operates in a very similar way to a lithium-ion battery, storing and releasing energy by moving charged ions between the positive and negative electrodes. The difference is simply that they use **sodium ions** **(Na⁺)** instead, which are larger than lithium ions, to move through the battery’s structure.

That difference in ion size and chemical properties influences everything from energy density and weight to efficiency and voltage behavior.

In practice, most commercial sodium-ion cells use a hard-carbon anode (not graphite) and sodium-based cathodes. To store a given amount of energy, sodium-ion cells must be larger and heavier than equivalent lithium-based cells.

They also rely on organic electrolytes, similar to lithium-ion batteries. This means sodium-ion is not inherently non-flammable and does not remove the need for a proper battery management system (BMS).

**In other words, sodium-ion does *not* guarantee a big safety advantage over lithium-iron-phosphate (LiFePO₄)-based packs.**

Broadly speaking, current sodium-ion cells offer:

* **Lower energy density** than LiFePO4 (they’re bulkier and heavier per kWh).
* **A wider voltage range** per cell.
* **A more “sloped” voltage curve**, meaning pack voltage steadily falls as the battery discharges.
* **Decent low-temperature charging capability** compared with standard lithium chemistries.

All of that is *interesting*. But the details matter a lot when you drop these batteries into a 12V or a 48V off-grid solar setup.

## The Deal-Breaker: Voltage Curve and Usable Capacity

Cycle life gets the headlines, but for RV, marine, and off-grid systems, battery voltage behavior is often the make-or-break factor.

When we look at how the batteries maintain voltage under load, sodium-ion chemistry performs poorly compared with LiFePO₄:

* During discharge, a sodium-ion battery’s voltage steadily drops as its state of charge decreases.
* Under moderate or heavy loads, that voltage drop becomes even more pronounced.

This behavior is comparable to older lead-acid batteries, which would sag deeply in voltage when running demanding equipment. Just as with lead-acid technology, this sag means **you often cannot use the full rated capacity of the battery** because your inverter will reach its low-voltage cutoff well before the battery is technically “empty.”

> *⚡️ Learn more about Voltage Drop here!*

LiFePO₄ is the opposite. It maintains a nearly flat voltage curve for most of the discharge cycle, even under substantial load. This stability means LifePo4 can use almost the entire rated capacity without prematurely tripping low voltage protection.

In practical terms, this translates to more usable watt-hours and a system that behaves consistently regardless of load.

> 💡 Yes, you *can* design special inverters, DC-DC conversion stages, or software tricks to get around this. But that adds:
>
> * Cost
> * Complexity
> * Another layer of “early adopter risk”
>
> For most boaters, RVers, and off-grid homeowners, that’s not a good trade.

| **Aspect** | **LiFePO₄ (LFP)** | **Sodium-Ion (Na-ion)** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Voltage Curve Shape** | Flat discharge curve; voltage remains stable through most of the cycle | Sloping linear curve; voltage steadily drops throughout the discharge cycle |
| **Voltage Stability Under Load** | Maintains high, consistent voltage even under moderate or heavy loads | More voltage sag under load due to higher internal resistance and changing reaction potential |
| **Operational Voltage Window** | Narrow, predictable voltage window (approx. 13.4 V full → ~12.8 V mid-range for a 12 V pack) | Much wider voltage window; full pack voltage may be >14 V and can fall below 10 V while still holding significant remaining state of charge |
| **Voltage Drop at Low State of Charge** | Drops sharply only near the bottom (2–5% SoC), allowing predictable depth of discharge | Voltage declines steadily, causing premature low-voltage conditions even at 40–60% state of charge |
| **Impact on Usable Capacity** | Nearly the entire rated capacity is usable before hitting inverter low-voltage cutoff | Actual usable capacity can be much lower than rated capacity because voltage reaches inverter cutoff early |
| **System Compatibility** | Ideal match for 12V / 24V / 48V inverter-based systems; stable voltage designed for modern power electronics | Often incompatible with standard inverters unless derated or specially configured due to large voltage swings |
| **Practical Outcome in RV/Off-Grid Use** | Predictable performance, consistent power delivery, and high utilization of battery Ah rating | Reduced usable watt-hours, inconsistent inverter operation, and significant performance loss under load |

## Why The Voltage Difference? A Look at the Chemical Reactions

We're battery nerds at heart, and our company's CEO is a battery chemist. So, we enjoy deep-diving into the technicals.

Voltage in any battery comes from the difference in electrochemical potential between the anode and the cathode. This potential difference is determined by the specific chemical reactions occurring at each electrode during charge and discharge. From an even more fundamental physics perspective, the potential is calculated from the **Gibbs free energy** change (ΔG) of the reaction.

Below are the actual redox reactions for **LiFePO₄ (LFP)** and **a typical sodium-ion chemistry,** and how those reactions translate into different voltages on the cell level. These underlying chemical behaviors explain the voltage instability and load sag observed in independent testing.

### LiFePO4 (LFP): The Reaction and Resulting Voltage

#### Cathode Reaction (LFP):

During discharge, lithium ions leave the anode (graphite) and insert into the LiFePO₄ cathode lattice. This reaction is:

**FePO₄ + Li⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ LiFePO₄**

This is a **two-phase reaction**, meaning LiFePO₄ transforms cleanly between two distinct crystalline phases (FePO₄ and LiFePO₄) without a lot of structural distortion.

That two-phase mechanism is why LiFePO₄ has such a **flat discharge curve** — the reaction potential stays almost constant throughout most of the charge/discharge cycle.

#### Anode Reaction (Graphite):

Lithium ions intercalate into graphite layers:

**C₆ ⇌ LiC₆ + e⁻ + Li⁺**

#### Cell Voltage:

To compute the voltage, we subtract the anode potential from the cathode potential.

* LiFePO₄ cathode potential: roughly **+3.45 V vs. Li⁺/Li**
* Graphite anode potential: roughly **+0.10 V vs. Li⁺/Li**

**Cell voltage ≈ 3.45 V − 0.10 V = ~3.35 V nominal**  
Fully charged limit is typically **3.65 V**.

This is why a 4-cell LiFePO₄ pack (4 × 3.2–3.3 V) produces a nominal **12.8–13.2 volts** and holds that voltage steadily across most of its usable capacity.

### Sodium-Ion: The Reaction and Resulting Voltage

There are multiple sodium-ion chemistries, but one of the most commercially relevant is **Prussian White / Sodium Iron Hexacyanoferrate (NaₓFe[Fe(CN)₆])**, used in many next-generation sodium-ion cells.

#### Cathode Reaction (Sodium-Ion Example):

**Na₁₋ₓFe[Fe(CN)₆] + xNa⁺ + xe⁻ ⇌ NaFe[Fe(CN)₆]**

This reaction inserts sodium ions into the Prussian white framework.

Unlike LiFePO₄, this is **not a clean two-phase reaction**. Structural changes occur gradually, so the reaction potential changes noticeably as sodium content changes.

This is why sodium-ion cells show a sloped voltage curve instead of a flat one.

#### Anode Reaction (Hard Carbon):

**C + xNa⁺ + xe⁻ ⇌ NaₓC**

Because sodium ions are much larger than lithium, they cannot intercalate into graphite — they instead insert into the pores of “hard carbon,” which has a much higher electrochemical potential than graphite.

Typical hard carbon potential: **~0.1–0.2 V vs. Na⁺/Na**

#### Cell Voltage:

* Typical cathode potential (Prussian White): **~3.3–3.4 V vs. Na⁺/Na**
* Hard carbon anode potential: **~0.1–0.2 V vs. Na⁺/Na**

**Cell voltage ≈ 3.3 V − 0.3 V ≈ 3.0 V nominal**  
Full charge may reach **3.8–4.0 V per cell**, depending on chemistry.

This lower nominal voltage is caused by the intrinsic electrochemical potential of sodium vs. lithium. Sodium sits higher on the periodic table, is less electronegative, and therefore produces a lower redox potential.

This is why a sodium-ion “12-volt” pack may require **4 or 8 cells in series** and still show a much larger voltage swing — for example:

* Full at **~14.4–15.2 V**
* Empty at **~8.0–9.5 V**

That wide voltage range is what causes inverter cutouts and poor usable capacity in 12/24/48V systems built around lithium chemistry.

## Sodium Ion Vs. Lithium Batteries: The Real-World Contrast

In addition to the major voltage issue discussed above, there are several main differences between sodium-ion batteries and lithium-ion batteries worth discussing:

### 1. Efficiency

Sodium-ion batteries currently exhibit lower overall efficiency compared to LiFePO₄. More energy is lost as heat during both charging and discharging due to higher internal resistance, which means more solar input or generator runtime is needed to achieve the same usable output.

In off-grid environments where every watt of solar harvest matters, this inefficiency becomes a meaningful drawback.

### 2. Cold Temperature Performance

Sodium-ion does have an interesting advantage: in cold temperatures, the chemistry can begin charging at lower temperatures than LiFePO₄, thanks in part to its hard-carbon anode design.

But because sodium-ion performance still suffers significantly at low temperatures during *discharge*, the cold-weather advantage is **not nearly as impactful as marketing materials sometimes suggest**.

While this characteristic is potentially valuable in very cold climates, LiFePO₄ batteries with built-in heating systems already solve this issue in a practical, well-proven way.

### 3. Cycle Life and Degradation

Cycle life is another area where sodium-ion has not yet matched the real-world endurance of LiFePO₄.

Although some manufacturers promote extremely high cycle-life numbers for optimized laboratory conditions, our own testing and broader industry data show that sodium-ion batteries tend to experience meaningful degradation far earlier than quality LiFePO₄ cells.

The reason for this partially has to do with the larger ionic size: Lithium ionic radius: ~0.76 angstroms (Å) , Sodium ionic radius: ~1.02 Å (roughly **35% larger**). Because the sodium-ion cathode is continuously expanding and contracting, the structure experiences more stress.

In mobile or off-grid use, where batteries experience variable depth-of-discharge cycles, fluctuating temperatures, and mixed charging sources, sodium-ion cells often drop in capacity sooner than expected.

LiFePO₄, by contrast, has an extensive track record of delivering thousands of cycles with predictable aging curves in exactly these real-world conditions. Our customers regularly achieve 3,000 to 5,000+ cycles with well-designed LiFePO₄ and see a decade or more of service life.

**The Takeaway:**

* In practice, many commercial sodium-ion cells today are in the **1,000–4,000 cycle** range before meaningful capacity loss.
* Quality LiFePO4 packs regularly deliver **3,000–5,000+ cycles** in real RV/off-grid service, and more when used gently and properly managed.

### 4. Weight, Size, and System Integration

Sodium-ion batteries currently carry a significant penalty in size and weight per kilowatt-hour. Because the chemistry stores less energy per pound than LiFePO₄, the resulting battery packs are bulkier and heavier.

In mobile applications—where payload, balance, and installation space matter—this is a major drawback. The additional size also means more difficulty integrating sodium-ion batteries into existing compartments, battery bays, or marine lockers.

### 5. Maturity & Ecosystem

Sodium-ion batteries are in the very early stages in consumer markets. In addition, they are not yet integrated into the broader 12-volt, 24-volt, and 48-volt ecosystem the way LiFePO₄ is.

Modern inverters, solar charge controllers, alternator charging systems, and DC-DC chargers are all optimized for LiFePO₄ profiles.

Sodium-ion, with its unusual voltage behavior and efficiency characteristics, would require redesigned system components to work reliably.

That ecosystem maturity matters enormously for installers, technicians, and consumers who rely on well-understood equipment standards.

### 6. Safety

Safety is a very important factor to compare between battery types. Let's take a look:

**LiFePO4** is already one of the most stable and safest lithium chemistries on the market.

* Highly resistant to thermal runaway
* Handles electrical abuse more predictably
* Maintains a stable voltage throughout discharge
* Proven safe in countless RVs, boats, and homes when installed correctly.

**Sodium-ion** *is* safer than many high-nickel lithium chemistries, but does not offer a meaningful safety advantage over LiFePO4 for low-voltage systems.

* Sodium-ion cells are generally safe and well-behaved when used as designed.
* Some sodium chemistries do offer good thermal stability and avoid certain high-energy, high-volatility cathode materials.
* Wider voltage swing can stress components and create more unpredictable shutdown or fault conditions
* But they still rely on similar organic electrolytes and require a robust BMS and proper design to mitigate abuse conditions (short circuits, overcharge, etc.).

At this time, sodium-ion just does not provide a clear, significant safety advantage over LiFePO4.

### 7. Cost Comparison

Sodium-ion is often promoted as a cheaper alternative to lithium batteries because sodium is abundant and inexpensive as a raw material.

* **Sodium-ion is not cheaper right now — in fact, many packs cost more than LiFePO₄.**  
  Real-world sodium-ion batteries currently on the market often cost *double* what an equivalent LiFePO₄ battery costs, despite the perception that sodium should be “cheap.”

* **Shipping costs wipe out much of the theoretical material savings.**  
  Because sodium-ion cells are larger and heavier per kilowatt-hour, shipping often costs more than the cells themselves, eliminating any raw-material advantage.

* **The “sodium is cheap” narrative doesn’t translate into cheap batteries.**  
  Although sodium is abundant, the *processing* and *manufacturing* infrastructure is still immature and concentrated in China, which keeps prices high. *(See the "Salt vs. Lithium" section below for more details)*

* **System-level costs widen that gap further.** Sodium-ion’s wide voltage range and sloped discharge curve can force earlier inverter shutoffs, requiring oversized packs, heavier cabling, or different power electronics to access the same usable energy. When you add in these integration costs, the total installed price can easily exceed that of LiFePO₄.

* **Cycle life also affects long-term economics.** High-quality LiFePO₄ regularly delivers **3,000–5,000+ cycles**, while current sodium-ion cells tend to degrade sooner under the deep-cycle patterns common in RV, marine, and off-grid systems.

**In short, low sodium-ion prices are not validated yet.** The marketing hype suggesting extremely low future sodium-ion prices is not reflected in any real commercial product today.

## Why Sodium-Ion Shows Promise in Other Markets

It is important to acknowledge that sodium-ion is not without merit. When used in large, stationary applications, such as utility-scale energy storage, where weight and size are irrelevant, and custom controllers can be built, the chemistry offers real long-term cost potential once global manufacturing ramps up.

Sodium-ion may also fit certain low-cost electric vehicle platforms in regions where compactness is less important than minimizing material costs. These are appropriate and promising use cases. But they are very different from the demands faced by an RV or a remote cabin reliant on an inverter-based electrical system.

## “Salt vs. Lithium": The Raw Materials Debate & What’s Actually in a Battery

A big part of the sodium-ion story is built around raw materials. Sodium is often presented as the “table salt” alternative to lithium, with claims that it will solve supply constraints and eliminate the need for “scarce” ingredients.

At a basic geologic level, that narrative has some truth to it. Sodium is roughly a thousand times more abundant than lithium in the Earth’s crust, and tens of thousands of times more plentiful in the oceans. In contrast, lithium is present at only a few parts per million in crustal rock and must be mined from brines or hard-rock deposits. On paper, that makes sodium an appealing building block for very large, long-term energy-storage deployments.

**However, there is an important distinction between elemental abundance and battery-grade material**. Sodium-ion batteries do not run on table salt from the grocery store. They rely on industrial sodium compounds such as soda ash (sodium carbonate) and specialized electrolyte salts that must be refined to tight purity specifications.

These compounds are indeed cheaper at the commodity level than lithium carbonate—hundreds of dollars per ton for sodium carbonate vs. thousands per ton for lithium carbonate in recent years—but they **still require a full mining, refining, and manufacturing chain**. And that chain is currently far less mature than lithium’s. In other words, sodium’s natural abundance does not automatically translate to instant, cheap, globally available sodium-ion battery packs.

It also helps to zoom in on how much lithium is actually used in a modern lithium iron phosphate battery. A 100 Ah, 12 V-class LiFePO₄ battery (about 1.2–1.3 kWh), contains **only a few hundred grams of lithium in total.**

In practical terms, the lithium fraction of the entire battery mass is modest. Most of the weight is made up of aluminum and copper current collectors, electrolyte, separator, casing, and, in the case of LiFePO₄, abundant elements like iron and phosphorus.

This is where LiFePO₄’s materials story becomes very compelling. Unlike many nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) or nickel-cobalt-aluminum (NCA) chemistries used in EV batteries, LiFePO₄ cathodes contain **no cobalt and no nickel** at all. They are based on lithium, iron, and phosphate: all relatively abundant, widely distributed, and well-understood materials. Cobalt in particular is associated with significant cost volatility and complex social and environmental concerns, which LiFePO₄ completely avoids. From a resource and ethics standpoint, that means **LiFePO₄ already solves many of the “rare metal” issues that sodium-ion marketing often implies it is uniquely positioned to address**.

At Battle Born (and our parent company Dragonfly), our R&D team follows this materials debate closely because it affects both long-term sustainability and customer confidence. From our perspective, LiFePO₄ already represents a very responsible balance: it leverages a manageable amount of lithium, eliminates cobalt and other high-risk metals from the cathode, and relies heavily on abundant elements like iron and phosphorus.

Sodium-ion may eventually help diversify the global battery landscape, especially at the grid scale. But it does not magically make LiFePO₄ “obsolete” on material grounds, nor does it change the fact that LiFePO₄ uses far fewer problematic materials than many other lithium chemistries in use today.

## Why LiFePO₄ Remains the Best Choice for Boats, RVs, and Off-Grid Living

After evaluating sodium-ion extensively, our position is clear: LiFePO₄ remains the most reliable, efficient, and proven deep-cycle chemistry for mobile and off-grid applications.

# Sodium-ion vs lithium-ion batteries: the complete guide to next-generation battery technology

We look at how sodium-ion batteries are emerging as a safer, more sustainable alternative to lithium-ion technology, with major manufacturers like CATL and BYD leading the charge in EV applications.

Liam Critchley,Contributing Writer

February 24, 2026

schedule16 Min Read

Sodium-ion batteries are emerging as a safer, more sustainable alternative to lithium-ion technology.Image: AI-generated.

## At a Glance

* Sodium-ion batteries can offer safer, cheaper lithium-ion alternatives
* Wide temperature range: -40°C to 70°C operational capability
* Market could reach $6.83 billion by 2034

Lithium-ion batteries have long been the go-to rechargeable battery technology for most electronic applications, but other options are creeping up behind them. While lithium-ion batteries have the most robust supply chain, built over decades of development and manufacturing, other batteries are being developed that are either safer or have higher energy density.

The lithium market dominance stems from lithium-ion batteries' high energy density and safety properties, but there are batteries that exceed the properties of lithium-ion batteries in both categories. One of the frontrunning options is sodium-ion batteries. Both sodium-ion and lithium-ion batteries belong to the broad class of metal-ion batteries, so they share similar battery chemistry. While there is not yet a robust supply chain for sodium-ion batteries, they are not only seen as a safer alternative, but as the raw materials are a lot more abundant than lithium—with geopolitical tensions and limited lithium refining sites driving up the price of lithium—they are starting to be seen as a viable alternative.

It has taken some time for sodium-ion batteries to become a commercially viable alternative because their electrode chemistry has been more difficult to optimise than lithium-ion batteries. While this has slowed commercial development of sodium-ion batteries somewhat, the market has started to develop in the last few years, and the future looks bright for sodium-ion battery technology. The developments to date are primarily driven by Chinese companies who have been working on this technology for many years, but there is the potential for a global sodium-ion battery market to emerge. This article looks at how the sodium-ion market is developing.

## What are sodium-ion batteries? The technology fundamentals

From a chemistry perspective, a sodium-ion battery is very similar to a lithium-ion battery in its structure and function. This is because sodium and lithium possess similar physicochemical properties as they are located next to each other in group 1 of the periodic table. All alkali metals have similar properties, but they also have different atomic sizes—something that is very important when it comes to battery chemistry.

Sodium-ion batteries contain two electrodes, the anode (negative electrode) and the cathode (positive electrode). These two electrodes are separated by the electrolyte, which enables ions to move between them, and by a membrane, known as the separator, which physically separates the two halves of the battery cell while still allowing ions to pass through and move between the electrodes.

In a lithium-ion battery, lithium ions move between the electrodes during charging and discharging. During charging, the lithium ions move from a lithium-based cathode to the graphite anode. This creates a potential difference that transfers electrons from the ions to the external circuit. During charging, ions receive electrons from an external circuit (such as plugging the battery into mains power), and they migrate back to the cathode. The ends when an end-of-charge voltage threshold is reached. In both charging and discharging, the ions move from one electrode, through the electrolyte and separator, to the other electrode.

In principle, a sodium-ion battery works almost identically to a lithium-ion battery and the sodium ions shuttle between the electrodes in the same manner as lithium ions under similar conditions. However, there are some marked differences due to the different chemistry of sodium ions. The cathode of a sodium-ion battery is a sodium-based cathode instead of a lithium cathode. That part has not been the issue to date for developing sodium-ion batteries.

The issue has been on the anode side, and this issue revolves around the point made earlier about the atomic size of sodium ions. The performance of a battery hinges on the capabilities of both the anode and cathode. One of the main reasons lithium-ion batteries have become ubiquitous is the very efficient, very stable graphite anode present in almost every lithium-ion battery. Graphite has a robust supply chain, and specific grades are specially processed for lithium-ion batteries.

However, graphite is not suitable for sodium-ion batteries because sodium ions are too large. Relatively speaking, sodium ions are still incredibly small, but they are too big for the pores of graphite (even though they can technically fit in). The difference between the radius size of lithium ions and sodium ions is only 0.3 nm (three 10-billionths of a metre), and this tiny increase has a big impact. Even though it seems like a very small difference, it makes the ions much heavier, essentially making the atomic weight of sodium ions over three times that of lithium ions, with an atomic mass unit (amu) of 22.99 amu for sodium and 6.94 amu for lithium.

Sodium ions are too big for the pores of graphite and are over three times the atomic weight of lithium ions. Image: AI-generated.

This increase in size and mass makes sodium ions thermodynamically unfavourable for graphite anodes and causes irreversible exfoliation reactions at the electrolyte-anode interface. When graphite is used, the battery can break down quickly. Additionally, heavier and larger ions cause more mechanical stress on the cell as they pass between the electrodes, so there is the possibility of the cells deteriorating rapidly if not managed properly—something that goes against the inherent safety of using sodium over lithium. This has been a challenge because if it is not considered, it can lead to shorter cycle lives.

The inability to use standard battery-grade graphite has slowed commercial production, as a scalable alternative needed to be found—most commonly, hard carbon materials to date. If graphite were suitable for sodium-ion batteries, it is likely that we would have already seen a much wider adoption of sodium-ion technology in commercial applications today, as the same fundamental supply chain could be used.

All new technologies undergo their own development, fine-tuning, and scalability challenges, and these issues have been unique challenges to sodium-ion batteries. The issues have often been more vocalised because they are being directly compared with lithium-ion, as they are so similar. Nevertheless, the similar battery chemistry means that battery engineers have been able to learn from the commercial and manufacturing issues of lithium-ion batteries, enabling challenges to be overcome more quickly than if engineers were investigating a completely new architecture.

Even with the many chemical and atomic-scale challenges of manufacturing safe and efficient sodium-ion batteries, companies have begun producing them on a commercial scale, and they are now being used in consumer applications—most notably in stationary storage and EV applications. Like any battery, sodium-ion batteries are defined by their performance and capabilities for a given application, and some naturally outperform others. Regardless of the battery in question, all sodium-ion batteries are governed by the following performance metrics:

Capacity (Ah): The amount of current that a battery provides over a given time. The capacity of a battery can be multiplied by its nominal voltage to determine the amount of energy it can store.

Charge/Discharge Rate (C-rate): The C-rate is a unitless ratio that determines how fast a battery charges and/or discharges (C-rates for charging and discharging can be different). The higher the C-rate, the higher the charge/discharge. For example, 1C means that a battery charges/discharges in 1 hour, whereas 2C is 30 minutes and 10C is 6 minutes.

Cycle Life: The number of charge and discharge cycles that a battery undergoes before its performance starts to degrade. The degradation is directly linked to the state of health (SoH) of the battery as a percentage, i.e., a 90% SoH means the battery has lost 10% of its initial capacity.

Gravimetric Energy Density (Wh/Kg): The amount of energy stored per unit of mass of the battery. Typically used when battery weight is a factor.

Volumetric Energy Density (kWh/m3): The amount of energy stored per unit of volume. Typically used when the amount of required space for the battery is a factor.

Overall, sodium-ion batteries are a cheaper and safer alternative to lithium-ion batteries for different commercial applications. Sodium-ion batteries don’t use any rare earth metals, so they are cheaper to produce, the materials can be found in abundance, and the materials are less likely to suffer from geopolitical tensions, meaning that businesses are less likely to get caught in the middle of price hikes and trade wars.

While the energy storage capabilities are not as high as lithium-ion, the other benefits of sodium-ion batteries are beneficial for different energy storage applications. One of the key benefits of sodium-ion batteries over lithium-ion batteries is their ability to operate over a much wider temperature range, making them a better alternative for starting EVs in cold conditions. With this in mind, we explain more about how the two compare in the following section.

## Sodium-ion battery vs lithium-ion: complete comparison

Both lithium-ion batteries and sodium-ion batteries have their advantages and disadvantages. It’s unlikely that sodium-ion batteries will replace lithium-ion batteries, but they will be used alongside them for certain applications. ## Leading sodium-ion battery manufacturers: market analysis

Sodium-ion batteries are still in a state of relative infancy compared to lithium-ion batteries, but commercial developments are still happening. As it stands, the scale is much smaller than lithium-ion, but there is plenty of room to grow, and the possibility exists that existing lithium-ion plants can be retrofitted to also produce sodium-ion batteries. If this happens, production and scale-up costs could be reduced by leveraging existing infrastructure, and companies that have started commercial production of sodium-ion batteries also produce lithium-ion batteries.

It’s likely, like much of the battery industry, that the market will grow out of China, as that is where the majority of sodium-ion battery development and production is located, with estimates that around . While there are some other smaller sodium-ion producers, the majority of the Chinese market (and in turn the global market) is driven by two companies that are the main manufacturers of sodium-ion batteries: CATL and BYD.

According to Precedence Research, the sodium-ion market could grow to USD$6.83 billion by 2034. While much of this will focus on China, the EU is trying to increase the adoption of sodium-ion batteries through more favourable policies. Germany is currently leading the way in Europe, but its production capacity currently falls a long way below China.

## CATL sodium-ion battery innovation and market position

CATL (Contemporary Amperex Technology Co.) is currently the world's largest manufacturer of sodium-ion batteries, and the CATL sodium-ion battery story began back in 2016. CATL released its first sodium-ion battery back in 2021 and has gone on to develop a range of sodium-ion and hybrid battery packs (that use both lithium-ion and sodium-ion technology) for EV and stationary storage applications.

In 2025, CATL launched the Naxtra series of batteries, which targeted various EV markets. This included the Naxtra Passenger EV Battery, the Naxtra 24V Heavy-Duty Truck Integrated Start-Stop Battery, and the Freevoy Dual-Power Battery. The Naxtra series became the first mass-produced sodium-ion battery and cemented CATL’s position as the leading sodium-ion manufacturer in the world—a market position that they have not relinquished to date.

Both Naxtra batteries are operational across a temperature range of -40 to 70°C, making them suitable for cold climates. They both have an energy density of 175 Whkg-1, life cycles up to 10,000 cycles, and a driving range of 400-500 km rivalling a lot of lower-end lithium-ion batteries. It’s been talked about that the next generation could go beyond 200 Whkg-1, with ranges of 500-600 km for pure EV vehicles and 300-400 km for hybrid vehicles, but these developments won’t happen until at least 2027.

The two Naxtra batteries share many capabilities but have been designed for different driving environments. For example, the EV Passenger battery has a 90% retention of capacity at -40 °C, and stable power delivery at temperatures as low as –50 °C. The 24V Start-Stop battery, on the other hand, has been designed for heavy-duty trucks, with an 8-year service life, the ability to start after being idle for a year, deep discharge across the total capacity, and one-click starting at -40 °C. In 2025, CATL’s sodium-ion battery was the first battery to pass the GB 38031-2025 Electric Vehicles Traction Battery Safety Requirements certification.

CATL's Naxtra battery maintains fast-charging performance across a temperature range of -40°C to 70°C. Image: CATL.

CATL has also developed hybrid systems that combine both sodium-ion and lithium-ion technology, called the Freevoy Dual-Power Battery. Using ‘self-forming anode technology’, CATL has been able to engineer a 60% energy density and 50% gravimetric energy density increase into the same battery pack space. The battery can utilise both energy zones (the sodium and lithium zones) to meet the driving demands of both daily urban driving and long-distance travel. In this series of batteries, CATL has developed dual-lithium battery technology, including LFP-LFP, LFP-NCM, and NCM-NCM dual-power batteries, as well as a Naxtra-LFP dual-power battery. The main function so far for the Naxtra dual power variant is to provide extended range for vehicles operating in cold conditions.

Coming in 2026, CATL is still making advancements with its sodium-ion technology. , creating the world’s first mass-produced passenger vehicle with sodium-ion technology. CATL will supply sodium-ion batteries for CHANGAN’s full portfolio, including the AVATR, Deepal, Qiyuan, and UNI brands.

Outside of commercial deals, engineers at CATL are still looking to further improve their technology. A study published in the journal Small used a tin alloy for the anode instead of hard carbon. The rationale is that hard carbon has a capacity of 250–300 mAh g⁻¹, whereas sodium-tin alloys can theoretically achieve 847 mAh g⁻¹, which could increase the energy density at the cell level. There have been challenges with using tin because it undergoes volumetric expansion (the anode expands) when sodium ions enter, but CATL has been looking into nanoengineering methods to alleviate these problems. The paper uses carbon encapsulation layers to take the brunt of mechanical strain and stabilise the electrode interface—an approach that has also been applied to stabilise silicon anodes in lithium-ion batteries, which are similarly notorious for undergoing volumetric expansion.

## BYD sodium-ion battery technology and applications

BYD (Build Your Dreams) is the 2nd-largest power battery manufacturer in the world, behind CATL, and is best known for its LFP blade batteries, which have become a staple design in its EVs. Last year, EV installations reached 194.8GWh, but BYD has also been developing sodium-ion batteries.

Even though it's known for its EVs, the first BYD sodium-ion battery came in 2024, a sodium-ion battery for utility storage applications that also uses the blade-like structure. These batteries had a storage capacity of 2.3 MWh, which was lower than that of their lithium-ion counterparts, but they could be operated safely at lower temperatures. The battery also had a nominal voltage of 1200V and a voltage range of 800V-1400V.

One of the most notable developments from BYD is the announcement that it has begun construction of a 30GWh sodium-ion gigafactory in China, which is set to be a major boost to the sodium-ion supply chain. Once operational, they plan to operate it alongside Huaihai, who manufacture electric two- and three-wheelers. BYD has previously showcased a range of forklift batteries, including one based on the sodium-ion blade cell (C613N), which has a low capacity density to reduce the weight-balancing cost of forklifts and is ideal for those operating in cold storage environments.

Moving into 2026, new BYD sodium-ion batteries are being developed and announced with a cycle life of 10,000 cycles. This will be BYD’s third generation of sodium-ion battery and aims to compete with LFP cells. The batteries use a layered oxide and polyanion system to stabilise the battery for high-temperature applications, such as EVs, but no further details have been given on the battery’s other specifications. So far, the energy density has not been disclosed, but this battery chemistry is also planned for use in light vehicle applications.

## Industrial applications and use cases for sodium-ion batteries

While lithium prices fluctuate, they are not yet high enough for sodium-ion batteries to outcompete LFP in many applications, but it has already become a cost-effective option for EVs and stationary storage applications in cold environments, as well as for lithium-sodium hybrid energy storage systems. If lithium prices continue to climb, sodium-ion batteries will become more feasible for broader use applications.

For stationary storage applications, sodium-ion batteries have a good balance of safety, performance in a range of environmental temperatures, and competitive lifespans. In stationary storage, the weight and size of the batteries is not an issue, so building an energy storage system with lower energy density batteries (and more cells) is not an adoption barrier. For stationary storage applications in high- or low-temperature environments, sodium-ion batteries offer a strong alternative to lithium-ion batteries.

For EVs, sodium-ion batteries offer fast charging, high safety, and a wide operating temperature range, making them suitable for EV use. Sodium-ion-powered EVs are already being developed (as noted above), but their ranges are shorter than those of state-of-the-art lithium-ion batteries. However, lower-end lithium-ion batteries have similar ranges, so sodium-ion batteries can be used now for short-range models, with the aim of producing long-range models in the future as energy density increases. There is also a sizeable market for two- and three-wheelers in South East Asia, China and India, alongside conventional EVs and trucks. There is also the option of retrofitting existing vehicles with sodium-ion batteries, potentially replacing lead-acid batteries in road vehicles and being used to electrify industrial vehicles, such as industrial trucks and airport ground vehicles.

## Market outlook and future of sodium-ion battery technology

Market adoption of sodium-ion batteries is slowly increasing, as is the mass production of sodium-ion batteries for different applications. Despite this, there is not a robust supply chain in place, unlike lithium-ion batteries, and this will take time to develop. Companies like BYD, who are building gigafactories, are going to be a key part of market expansion, and the market is going to predominantly centre around China and the expansion from China—as no other region comes close in terms of sodium-ion battery performance and production capabilities.

There are companies in Europe, the US, and other parts of the world building prototypes, but it will still be some time before we see large-scale production in these regions. If we are to see major production levels in any region, building the supply chain is key. But it is a bit of a chicken-and-egg situation: without the supply chain, large-scale production will be difficult and cost-prohibitive; without regional demand, the supply chain won’t develop.

Supply chains developing across different regions will likely hinge on Chinese companies introducing sodium-ion technology to those regions or on European vehicles equipped with Chinese sodium-ion technology. Once the demand for local production has been established, the supply chain can be built, and wider market expansion can take place.

Significant growth is expected in the coming years. It will start with smaller end-use cases, but it’s likely that sodium-ion batteries will be integrated into a lot more products in the coming years as the technology matures. According to the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), global capacity could expand to 400GWh per year by 2030, and while estimates vary, they all indicate growth in the sodium-ion market in the coming years.

Regardless of development timelines, sodium-ion technology is now at a maturity level where it can start to challenge some lithium-ion chemistries, and as it continues to develop, it will be seen as a more feasible option for safe, more sustainable energy storage devices.
